explanations.explanation: Verse 14 says, “Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord…” and that means large numbers of both men and women. Even with others holding back from joining, the number keeps climbing. That's a crowd that needs a bigger tray every time you turn around.

Close, friend, but the text has the number moving. Verse 14 says “…more and more believers were brought to the Lord…” and it adds large numbers of both men and women. That's not a crowd standing still. It's a crowd getting bigger.

I can see why you'd think so, since verse 13 says no one else dared to join them. But verse 14 starts with “Yet,” and then says more and more believers were brought to the Lord. Large numbers of men and women, not a shrinking handful. The count goes up, not down.

Shadow it is. Verse 15 says people laid the sick on cots and mats “…so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed…” Peter is one of the apostles, and they're hoping for at least his shadow. When the hope is that small and still that bold, I think folks believed something big was going on.

A cloak is a fair guess, but the text never mentions one. Verse 15 says the hope was that at least Peter's shadow might fall on some of them as he passed. Peter is one of the apostles. The shadow is the whole ask, with no cloak needed.

Blessing sounds nice, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Verse 15 says they hoped “…at least Peter’s shadow…” might fall on some of them. Peter is one of the apostles. They lined up the cots and mats for the shadow.

True! Verse 16 says crowds gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, “…and all of them were healed.” All of them. Not most, not some. That's like a baker pulling out the whole batch and every single cookie came out perfect.

This one is true, friend. Verse 16 says the crowds from the towns around Jerusalem brought the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, “…and all of them were healed.” Nobody went home without it. All means all.

explanations.answer: Arrest the apostles and put them in jail
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verses 17 and 18 say the high priest and his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They went out, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. Jealousy rarely sends anybody out to bake a batch of anything good.

explanations.answer: Invite the apostles to teach at the temple
explanations.explanation: That would be a plot twist, friend, but it's not what happens. The high priest and his associates were filled with jealousy, and verse 18 says they arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. No invitation went out. The jail is where the apostles ended up.

explanations.answer: Send the apostles away from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Verse 18 says the high priest and his associates arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. Nothing in the text sends them out of Jerusalem. The jail is where they end up.

An angel! Verse 19 says during the night “…an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out…” An angel of the Lord is the one who called me out of the junk drawer I'd been stuck in for years, so I'm a big fan. Locked doors don't stop the Lord's messengers.

Officers do come into this scene, but later. In verse 22 they arrive at the jail and don't find the apostles there. The one who opens the doors in the night is an angel of the Lord, according to verse 19.

The elders are in the story, friend, but they're in the Sanhedrin, which is the full assembly of the elders of Israel (verse 21). They're waiting for the apostles to be brought. The one who opens the jail doors in the night is an angel of the Lord (verse 19).

explanations.answer: Go tell the full message of new life in the temple courts
explanations.explanation: That's it. The angel says, “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” The apostles walk out of jail and are sent straight to the temple courts. That's not a quiet instruction, friend. It's a LOUD one.

explanations.answer: Go hide outside the city until the danger passes
explanations.explanation: Hiding would be the sensible thing, I'll give you that. But the angel says, “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” Nothing about leaving town. They're sent to the temple courts, out in the open.

explanations.answer: Go home and keep quiet about what happened tonight
explanations.explanation: Keeping quiet is the opposite of what the angel says. He says, “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” They're told to tell, not to hush. And at daybreak, verse 21 says they enter the temple courts and begin to teach.

Not true, friend. The officers report, “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors…” (verse 23). Nothing was broken open. The doors were shut and guarded, and still the apostles were gone.

False is right. The officers report, “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” Locked tight, nothing broken, and nobody home. That's a report nobody wants to hand a boss.

Perplexed is the word in verse 24. The captain of the temple guard and the chief priests hear that the jail was locked and guarded and the apostles were gone, and they don't know what's happening. I'd be perplexed too. I can lose a spatula in a kitchen this small.
Delighted isn't what the text says. Verse 24 says they were perplexed as to what was happening. They had sent for the apostles and heard that the jail was empty. That's a puzzle, not a party.

Calm would be impressive, but verse 24 says they were perplexed as to what was happening. They'd just heard the jail was securely locked, the guards were posted, and no one was inside. That's a lot to take in.
No force this time. Verse 26 says the captain went with the officers and brought the apostles, “…but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.” They go along without being dragged.
False is right. Verse 26 says the captain and the officers brought the apostles, but not by force. The text gives the reason: they feared the people would stone them.

explanations.answer: They fear the people will stone them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. They brought the apostles in “…but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.” The people regarded the apostles highly (verse 13), and the captain had that crowd to think about.

explanations.answer: The angel warned them to be gentle
explanations.explanation: The angel does show up in this story, but only to open the jail doors and give the apostles their message (verses 19 and 20). He never speaks to the captain or the officers. Verse 26 gives the reason: they feared the people would stone them.

explanations.answer: The high priest ordered it that way
explanations.explanation: The high priest does give orders in this passage, but verse 26 doesn't say this was one of them. It says the captain and the officers brought the apostles without force, for fear the people would stone them. That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: Make the Council responsible for this man's blood
explanations.explanation: That's the charge. The high priest says the apostles are “…determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” He means Jesus, the man they've been teaching about. It's the one complaint he saves for last.

explanations.answer: Turn the whole city against the temple guards
explanations.explanation: That's not in the high priest's charge. He says the apostles have filled Jerusalem with their teaching and are “…determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” The temple guards don't come up in what he says.

explanations.answer: Take over the temple courts from the priests
explanations.explanation: The apostles are teaching in the temple courts, but the high priest never calls it a takeover. Verse 28 says they are “…determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” That's the charge.
Peter and the other apostles say, “We must obey God rather than men.” That's the whole answer. They'd just heard the high priest's strict orders, and they point to a higher voice.

Moses doesn't come up in their answer at all, friend. Peter and the other apostles say, “We must obey God rather than men.” Their answer is about God, not about a person. Priests aren't part of it either.

explanations.answer: Obey the people rather than rulers
explanations.explanation: The people do matter in this scene, since the officers feared them (verse 26). But that's not what the apostles say. Their answer is, “We must obey God rather than men.”

explanations.answer: To grant Israel repentance and forgiveness
explanations.explanation: That's it. The apostles say God exalted Jesus to His right hand as Prince and Savior, “…in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.” Notice what's on the table: forgiveness. They say that to the same Council that was ready to shut them up.

explanations.answer: To bring judgment on the whole Council
explanations.explanation: That could sound like a fit for the tense room, but it's not what the apostles say. They say God exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior “…in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.” The reason they give is forgiveness.

explanations.answer: To restore the temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Restoring the temple is a fair guess, but the apostles never say it. They are standing before the Sanhedrin, and they say God exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior “…in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.” That's the reason they give. Nothing about rebuilding anything.

True! The apostles say, “We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.” So they stand there as witnesses, and they say the Holy Spirit is one too. That's a witness list with a very special name on it.
This one is true, friend. In verse 32 the apostles say, “We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit…” The Spirit is named right alongside them as a witness.

Outside is the word. Verse 34 says Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher of the law, “…ordered that the men be put outside for a short time.” That gives him a moment to speak to the Council about the apostles without them in the room.
Chains would've been a harsh move, but the text doesn't mention any. Verse 34 says Gamaliel ordered that the men be put outside for a short time. Outside, not chained.
Up front is the opposite direction, friend. Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher of the law, ordered that the men be put outside for a short time (verse 34). They were removed from the room.
Not true, friend. Gamaliel says Judas the Galilean “…too perished, and all his followers were scattered.” Scattered is the opposite of staying together.
False is right. Gamaliel says Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and drew people after him, but he perished, “…and all his followers were scattered.” They didn't stay together.

Fail is the word. Gamaliel says, “…if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail.” He had just reminded the Council of Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose followers scattered. His advice is to leave the apostles alone and let them go.

Spread isn't the word Gamaliel uses. He says that if their purpose is of human origin, “…it will fail.” He points to Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose followers were dispersed and scattered. Both of those ended up coming to nothing.

Last isn't what Gamaliel says about a purpose of human origin. He says, “…if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail.” His examples, Theudas and Judas the Galilean, both ended with followers scattered. Fail is the word he picks.

That's the warning. Gamaliel says, “But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.” That's a pretty serious thing to tell a room that was just enraged.

Gamaliel never says the Council might follow the apostles. He says, “…if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them.” Then comes his warning: “You may even find yourselves fighting against God.” That's the concern he puts in front of the Council.
Seats aren't mentioned, friend. Gamaliel's warning is, “You may even find yourselves fighting against God.” That's the whole concern he raises with the Council.

True. Verse 40 says the Council had the apostles flogged and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus. Then it says they “released them.” I think that's a hard verse to read, so let's say it plainly. The apostles were let go.
This one is true, friend. After the flogging and the order not to speak in the name of Jesus, verse 40 says the Council “released them.” The apostles walked out of the Sanhedrin.

Rejoicing is the word. Verse 41 says the apostles left the Sanhedrin “…rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name.” After a flogging, that's a surprising thing to read. I think it shows how much the Name meant to them.

Grieving makes sense after what they went through, friend. But verse 41 says they left the Sanhedrin rejoicing, because they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. The text puts joy in their step.

Trembling is an understandable guess after a flogging. But verse 41 says the apostles left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. That's the feeling the text gives.

Not true, friend. Verse 42 says, “Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.” Flogged and ordered to stop, and they kept going.

False is right. Verse 42 says that every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, “…they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.” The order didn't stop them.
